Background Process heating accounts for most of the overall energy footprint of the industrial manufacturing sector. Industrial process heat (IPH) is primarily supplied by combustion of greenhouse gas (GHG) emitting natural gas and other fossil fuels. Up to 60% of the process heat demand (~6500 TBtu) in US manufacturing industries falls in the medium temperature range of 100-250 oC [1,2]. Industries that require heat in this temperature range include chemical production, ethyl alcohol manufacturing, non-metallic mineral production (e.g. soda ash, potash, and borax mining), and food processing. In addition, the heat demand for thermal enhanced oil recovery (TEOR) operations [3] in US that requires steam in this temperature range is ~200 TBtu, often supplied by natural gas fueled once-through steam generators. To meet this demand, adoption of cost effective and commercially proven line- focusing concentrating solar thermal (CST) technologies such as parabolic trough and linear Fresnel offer promising solutions. These systems can operate at temperatures up to 310 °C using safer, non-corrosive, food-grade mineral oil as heat transfer fluids, making them attractive for adoption in the risk-averse manufacturing sector [4]. However, energy supply from solar is intermittent and only available during the day, while the operation of most industrial processes requires continuous energy supply to meet the 24/7 load requirement. Hence, integration of low-cost thermal energy storage (TES) is critical to make solar energy dispatchable by storing excess heat during peak solar periods and meet the process heat demand when solar is unavailable. This increases system reliability and reduces the dependency on fossil fuel backup and can enable lower levelized cost of heat (LCOH) than that of natural gas boiler. The most common hot TES uses high-cost solar salt (between $1000-$1200/ton), in two-tank configurations. The widespread implementation of molten nitrate salt TES is in concentrating solar power plants [5]. Typically, in a two-tank system, molten nitrate salt flows through heat exchanger to transfer heat process fluid as it flows between hot tank and cold tank. The strength of molten salt TES is that the salts are liquid in the operating temperature range for power generation, allowing for it to have good charge/discharge efficiency and heat transfer rate through heat exchangers.
